metadata.title: Literacy Skills for the World of Tomorrow (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report describes PISA 2000 as a large-scale, internationally comparable assessment of 15-year-olds, implemented with standardized procedures across participating countries. It uses sampling of students and booklets so that each student receives a subset of items, and it reports uncertainty via standard errors and confidence intervals. For school-level questionnaire responses, the report states that principal responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school. The report does not provide a student weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the extracted text, so the exact weighting variables used for student-level estimates cannot be specified here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an OECD/PISA results report chapter describing assessment design, proficiency levels, and descriptive cross-country distributions rather than an empirical predictive analysis with a specified PV-based dependent variable. Plausible values handling is therefore not applicable to the extraction target (no ML model predicting PV-based outcomes is estimated in the provided text). Missing-data handling is not reported at the level of an analytic ML pipeline (e.g., imputation vs deletion rules), because the chapter focuses on reporting PISA results and methodological guidance rather than specifying a missing-data strategy for an empirical model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report defines the PISA target population as 15-year-olds aged between 15 years 3 months and 16 years 2 months at the beginning of the assessment period, enrolled in educational institutions (excluding 15-year-olds not enrolled). It states that, with the exception of Brazil, Luxembourg and Poland, at least 95% of the target population was covered by the actual samples, and more than 97% in most countries. The assessment uses booklets where each student receives a subset of items, and it reports that principal questionnaire responses are weighted to reflect the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in each school. No additional analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., grade-only, module-only, complete-case rules) are specified in the extracted text for this chapter.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report chapter summarizes PISA 2000 results for reading literacy (and provides methodological background on PISA assessment design). PISA 2000 used pencil-and-paper tests with a total assessment time of two hours per student and a background questionnaire administered for about half an hour (students) plus a school principal questionnaire. The reading literacy domain is assessed using a pool of reading tasks (about 141 tasks) arranged along a difficulty continuum estimated with Item Response Theory, and proficiency is reported on a combined reading literacy scale anchored to an OECD mean of 500 (SD 100). Because each student receives a subset of tasks, the report presents population estimates with uncertainty (standard errors and confidence intervals) and uses proficiency levels (Levels 1–5) to benchmark performance. The chapter reports cross-country distributions (e.g., percentages at or above Level 3/Level 5) and discusses policy-relevant implications of low performance (below Level 1) and within-country variation, while cautioning that causal interpretations are limited by the observational nature of the assessment.
